title: Stringing a bow
hookLine: heaven's way is like stringing a bow: it lowers the high and raises the low (Tao Te Ching 77)
last: THE SOFT AND YIELDING ARE COMPANIONS OF LIFE.

cards: To string a bow, an archer braces one tip against the ground and bends the wood.

The top comes down, the bottom comes up, the string slips into its notch, and suddenly a curved stick is a tool with tension and balance from end to end. It's a small, practical motion, done without thinking.
Chapter seventy-seven of the Tao Te Ching watches it and says: that's how heaven works.

teach.b: First, the bow. Isn't heaven's way like stringing a bow? the chapter asks. What's high is pressed down; what's low is lifted up.
Readers picture it two ways: bending the bow to string it, or adjusting the string so the aim comes true. Either way, the motion evens things out.

teach.h: TAKE FROM TOO MUCH, GIVE TO TOO LITTLE.
teach.b: Second, the rule, said plainly: heaven's way takes from what has too much and gives to what has too little. Third, the contrast. The way of people, the chapter goes on, isn't like that.
It takes from those who don't have enough to give to those who already have too much. Then a question: who can take what they have in excess and offer it to the world? Only someone who has the Tao.
It sets heaven's way and the human habit side by side and lets the gap speak.
Fourth, the sage, who acts without holding on, finishes the work without staying to claim it, and has no wish to show off his worth.
That's giving from the top of the bow done well: quietly, without a plaque.

Day to day, it's less about grand charity than about noticing where things have piled up in your own life, extra time, extra chairs, extra coats in the closet, extra patience on a good day, and where, nearby, something is running low.

how: Readers of the Tao Te Ching often take chapter seventy-seven's bow as a picture of balance: heaven's way takes from excess to supply lack, and the sage gives from surplus without claiming credit.

o: a test of strength used to choose the next ruler
an archer's skill that only soldiers need to learn
heaven's way: pressing down the high, lifting the low

p: takes from too much, gives to too little
takes from too little, gives to too much

s: chapter seventy-seven says the way of people matches heaven's way
it says the human habit runs backward: taking from those who lack to give to those with too much.
the chapter compares heaven's way to stringing a bow
the high is pressed down and the low lifted up.
the sage in chapter seventy-seven stays to claim the finished work
the sage finishes the work without staying to claim it.

games.q: you have more than you need. chapter seventy-seven asks a question about people like you. what is it?
o: how can you keep it safe?
who can take their excess and offer it to the world?
why do others have so little?
games.why: the chapter asks who can offer their excess to the world, and answers: only someone who has the Tao.

practice: Let the breath even out, like a bow finding balance, and take a quiet inventory of what you have more of than you use: things, yes, but also time, skill, attention, a spare room, a kind word.
Then let one person or place come to mind that's running short of exactly that. Hold the two together, the high and the low, and let a small way to bring them level take shape.

wordCard.voice: Stringing a bow. Chapter seventy-seven: heaven's way presses down the high and lifts the low, taking from too much to give to too little. Today's word.
